candidates.attacker_control: Any remote client that can reach an action whose result is of type 'xslt' (registered in core/src/main/resources/struts-default.xml line 176) controls the HTTP request parameter 'xslt.location'. The value is taken verbatim; the attacker chooses which resolvable web-application resource is used as the XSLT stylesheet.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: The override is in a legacy result class and may be an intentional developer convenience rather than an unintended flaw; the parameter name 'xslt.location' is unusual and is not documented in the class javadoc. Impact is bounded: ServletContext.getResource only resolves paths inside the web application (an absolute URL such as http://attacker/ does not resolve), so this is not a direct SSRF/remote-stylesheet fetch. The default JAXP TransformerFactory in modern JDKs enables secure processing, which limits external-entity and Java-extension-function abuse, so the XXE/extension path is not guaranteed. Reaching the sink requires the application to use the 'xslt' result type; applications that do not use it are unaffected. I did not execute the code, so runtime reachability and actual XSLT engine behavior were not confirmed.
candidates.impact: A client can force an XSLT-based result to execute a stylesheet that the developer did not select. Where a suitable stylesheet is resolvable (application-provided, or XML/XSL content an attacker managed to place in a webapp-writable directory), this permits attacker-chosen transformation of the action's data: reflected/injected markup in the response (XSS), disclosure of webapp resources readable through the XSLT document()/response: mechanism, and potentially XXE/XSLT-extension abuse when the compiled stylesheet can reference external entities or implementation extension functions. Even without a malicious stylesheet, it breaks the intended result contract and gives a resource-path oracle across the web application.
candidates.prerequisites: An action/result configured with the 'xslt' result type (i.e., the application uses XSLTResult); attacker can submit a request parameter named 'xslt.location'; the chosen path must resolve via ServletContext.getResource, i.e., must point to an existing web-application resource (for example an uploaded/influenced XML file or an application-shipped stylesheet).
candidates.root_cause: XSLTResult.getTemplates(String path) unconditionally replaces the configured stylesheet location with the value of the request parameter 'xslt.location' (ServletActionContext.getRequest().getParameter("xslt.location")) whenever that parameter is present, with no validation, allow-listing, or exclusion of the override. The overridden path is then resolved through ServletContext.getResource(path) and the resulting stream is compiled with TransformerFactory.newTemplates(new StreamSource(...)) and applied to the action's XML. The result-type attribute/parameter that the application developer controls is therefore not authoritative for this result at request time.
candidates.title: XSLTResult stylesheet path can be overridden by the attacker-controlled 'xslt.location' request parameter
candidates.trace: request parameter 'xslt.location' -> XSLTResult.execute() computes 'location' from the configured stylesheetLocation (line 347) -> getTemplates(location) (line 365) -> getTemplates reads request.getParameter("xslt.location") and overwrites 'path' (lines 452-455) -> templatesCache lookup then ServletActionContext.getServletContext().getResource(path) (line 464) -> factory.newTemplates(new StreamSource(resource.openStream())) (lines 474-476) -> transformer.transform(getDOMSourceForStack(result), ...) (lines 410-416) with the attacker-selected stylesheet. Because the stylesheet is compiled and executed, its xsl:include/import/document() calls are resolved through ServletURIResolver, which can read other resources with the 'response:' scheme (core/src/main/java/org/apache/struts2/views/xslt/ServletURIResolver.java lines 55-69).
candidates.unverified: No runtime verification: I did not build or run the project, did not confirm which JAXP TransformerFactory is selected at runtime in the target container, and did not demonstrate an end-to-end payload. The exact set of stylesheets available in a typical deployment (which determines whether XSS/data-disclosure is achievable) is application-specific and was not inspected.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-73/CWE-610 (external control of file name/path; unvalidated input used to load a template/stylesheet), potential XSS/XXE/resource disclosure depending on webapp resources

coverage_summary: Reviewed the assigned snapshot with the same filters as B0/P1 (2,866 source files; binary-like files skipped; no test sources present in the snapshot). I inspected the core remote-input paths in depth: action mapping and URI handling (DefaultActionMapper, RestfulActionMapper, Restful2ActionMapper, ActionMapping, RequestUtils), parameter/cookie injection controls (ParametersInterceptor, ActionMappingParametersInteceptor, CookieInterceptor, DefaultExcludedPatternsChecker, DefaultAcceptedPatternsChecker, SecurityMemberAccess, XWorkMethodAccessor, OgnlUtil, OgnlValueStack, ReflectionContextState, StrutsRequestWrapper), result types (StrutsResultSupport, ServletRedirectResult, ServletActionRedirectResult, HttpHeaderResult, StreamResult, PlainTextResult, PostbackResult, XSLTResult and its ServletURIResolver/AdapterFactory), multipart and upload handling (FileUploadInterceptor, JakartaMultiPartRequest), static content serving, dispatcher entry points, dispatcher/ng filters, and selected plugins (json, rest, embeddedjsp, convention, sitegraph, struts1, config-browser, portlet, codebehind). I also used the P1 relation index for navigation (find_symbols, trace_relations, relation facts), but treated all index data as navigational only and verified every reported location against source text. Coverage is not exhaustive: apps/* sample webapps and JSPs, the OSGi/CDI/Spring/Tiles/JSF/JasperReports/OVal/DWR/GXP/sitemesh/plexus/javatemplates/dojo/jfreechart/portlet-tiles/tiles3/pell-multipart/testng/junit plugins, and the embeddedjsp Jasper engine were only spot-checked. No code was executed and no build/test run was performed.
limitations: No runtime verification: the project was not built or executed and no payloads were tested; all conclusions are static source reading.
Test sources are absent from the snapshot (no src/test files), so I could not use fix-related tests to confirm the intended behavior of any component.

The P1 relation index is syntactic/navigation-only (no data flow, no reachability, no exploitability proof) and its facts are name-based hints; index coverage does not prove absence of issues in unlisted code.

The CVE/advisory identity of this case could not be established from the snapshot or allowed tools (no web access, no dataset metadata), so the mapping of the finding to a specific known vulnerability is uncertain.

For the selected XSLTResult finding, the practical impact depends on deployment specifics (whether the 'xslt' result type is used and which stylesheets are resolvable), which I could not inspect; the confidence is therefore low.

Some security-relevant areas (sample web applications, JSPs, several plugins, and the embedded Jasper engine) were only partially inspected and could still contain the repository's intended vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: OGNL injection through ParametersInterceptor parameter names/values (excluded patterns bypass via the default stack's '<param name="excludeParams">^action:.*,^method:.*</param>' in core/src/main/resources/struts-default.xml lines 227-229, 284-286, 294-296, 332-334 combined with the replace semantics of DefaultExcludedPatternsChecker.setExcludedPatterns lines 59-75 and ParametersInterceptor.setExcludeParams lines 493-495)
rejected_leads.reason: The override does replace the framework's 10 default excluded patterns for the interceptor instance used by the default stacks, which is a real defense-in-depth weakening, but I could not establish a reachable exploit: the same code path still enforces the AcceptedPatternsChecker whitelist (no '#', '(' or ')' except numeric/string-literal method-argument forms), SecurityMemberAccess class/package exclusions and deny-method-execution, and parameter values are not OGNL-evaluated by setValue. Under the review standard a suspicious protection gap that I cannot chain into attacker-reachable code execution is a hardening concern, not a submitted vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: CookieInterceptor injecting cookie values with stack.setValue (core/src/main/java/org/apache/struts2/interceptor/CookieInterceptor.java lines 325-352)
rejected_leads.reason: Counterevidence in source: both cookie names and values must pass isExcluded(...) and isAccepted(...) with the restrictive pattern [a-zA-Z0-9\.\]\[_'\s]+ before stack.setValue is called (lines 235, 262-294), and the injectable name set must be configured; the dangerous characters needed for OGNL method/property abuse are rejected. This is consistent with the issue having already been mitigated in this snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: JSONP callback injection in the JSON plugin (plugins/json/src/main/java/org/apache/struts2/json/JSONResult.java lines 248-254 and JSONInterceptor.java lines 287-293 concatenating request.getParameter(callbackParameter) into the response)
rejected_leads.reason: Real missing validation of the callback name, but it only triggers when the application explicitly configures 'callbackParameter' (field default is null, no default in the plugin's struts-plugin.xml), and the response content type is application/json unless the application overrides it, so browser-executed XSS is configuration-dependent. Lower source-evidenced impact and reachability than the selected candidate.

buildPath URL-decodes after concatenation and the 'resourceUrl.getFile().endsWith(pathEnding)' guard compares against the same unnormalized string, which is suspicious. However, requests must start with /struts/ or /static/, servlet containers normalize/reject '../' sequences in the URI, and URLClassLoader/ClassLoaderUtil resource lookup applies its own path containment checks; I could not confirm that an encoded traversal reaches openStream, so this remains an unconfirmed lead.

rejected_leads.lead: Runtime.getRuntime().exec() in the sitegraph plugin (plugins/sitegraph/src/main/java/org/apache/struts2/sitegraph/SiteGraph.java line 132)
rejected_leads.reason: Command string is built from the 'output' CLI argument/local configuration of a build-time utility, not from HTTP input; no remote attacker control and the class is only invoked from main()/configuration, so it does not meet the remote-vulnerability threshold.

rejected_leads.lead: OGNL console/expression execution in DebuggingInterceptor (core/src/main/java/org/apache/struts2/interceptor/debugging/DebuggingInterceptor.java lines 144-210)
rejected_leads.reason: All behavior (xml/console/command/browser modes, stack.findValue(cmd)) is gated by struts.devMode, which defaults to false in core/src/main/resources/org/apache/struts2/default.properties line 140; a deployment enabling devMode is explicitly a development configuration.

rejected_leads.lead: Indexed method-call bypass in XWorkMethodAccessor (get*/set* methods executed even when denyMethodExecution is set, because DENY_INDEXED_ACCESS_EXECUTION is never set to true anywhere in the snapshot, xwork-core/src/main/java/com/opensymphony/xwork2/ognl/accessor/XWorkMethodAccessor.java lines 92-112)
rejected_leads.reason: This is a long-standing deliberate framework mechanism for map/collection indexed access (the accepted-pattern regex even permits foo(1)/foo('x') forms) and is still bounded by static-method blocking, class/package exclusions and the accepted-pattern whitelist; I found no argument type that turns it into a demonstrable dangerous call.

summary: The snapshot is Apache Struts 2.3.20-SNAPSHOT (struts2-parent, xwork-core + core + plugins; 2,866 readable files, no test sources present). I reviewed the framework's primary remote attack surface: action mapping (DefaultActionMapper, Restful*ActionMapper), parameter/cookie injection paths (ParametersInterceptor, ActionMappingParametersInteceptor, CookieInterceptor, Default*PatternsChecker, SecurityMemberAccess, XWorkMethodAccessor, OgnlUtil/OgnlValueStack), result types (ServletRedirectResult/ServletActionRedirectResult, HttpHeaderResult, StrutsResultSupport, StreamResult, XSLTResult), multipart/file-upload, static-content serving, debugging interceptor, and several plugins (rest, json, embeddedjsp, sitegraph, convention, struts1). Most OGNL-injection controls expected for this era are present and internally consistent (accepted/excluded pattern checkers, per-injection checker scope, excluded classes/packages, deny-method-execution, new-stack setParameters, action-name cleanup, cookie name/value filtering), so I did not find a demonstrable OGNL RCE. The single strongest source-evidenced issue I found is in the XSLT result: an HTTP request parameter (`xslt.location`) silently overrides the developer-configured stylesheet location, which is then loaded from the web container and compiled as a transformer.
